skill.name: building-agent-tools
skill.description: Guidance for designing agent-facing tools, MCP interfaces, and APIs with clear names, efficient outputs, and useful error handling.
skill.summary: Design practical tools that AI agents can understand, call, and recover from efficiently.
skill.author: Byunk

security_audit.summary: The static findings are false positives from inline markdown code examples and ordinary design guidance in SKILL.md. No executable scripts, shell command instructions, reconnaissance behavior, prompt injection, or malicious intent were found.

static_findings.snippet: - Example: `schedule_event` that checks availability AND creates event
- Prefix related tools with service name: `asana_projects_search`, `asana_users_search`
- Use descriptive `name` and `description` in tool schema
- Define `inputSchema` with JSON Schema for parameters
- Avoid simple CRUD-style tools that require multiple calls
- Include parameter constraints and valid values

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 35 contains an inline markdown tool name example, not Ruby or shell execution. There is no executable code or instruction to run a command.
Line 39 uses inline markdown code formatting for sample tool names. The text explains naming conventions and does not invoke external commands.
Line 46 formats a parameter name with markdown backticks. It describes an API option and contains no command execution path.
Line 73 formats schema field names with markdown backticks. The content is documentation guidance, not executable shell or Ruby syntax.
Line 74 formats inputSchema as an inline code term. It advises using JSON Schema and does not execute or request external commands.
Line 36 advises against overly granular CRUD-style tools. It does not request system discovery, host enumeration, or environment inspection.
Line 58 recommends documenting parameter constraints and valid values. This is API design guidance, not system reconnaissance.

content.value_statement: Agent-facing tools often fail when names, inputs, and outputs are unclear. This skill helps Claude, Codex, and Claude Code users design efficient tool interfaces.
actual_capabilities: Explains a workflow for defining, designing, implementing, and validating agent tools.
Recommends namespacing patterns for related tool families.
Shows how to reduce token usage with filtering, pagination, and concise outputs.
Describes MCP tool registration fields and input schema expectations.
Identifies common anti-patterns in agent tool design.
limitations: Does not provide executable implementation code.
Does not validate a real MCP server or API at runtime.
Does not cover authentication, authorization, or deployment security.
Does not replace user testing with real agent workflows.

use_cases.title: Plan a New MCP Tool
use_cases.description: Define a tool purpose, interface, parameters, and output format before implementation begins.

use_cases.title: Improve an Existing Agent API
use_cases.description: Review tool names, response shape, pagination, filtering, and error messages for agent use.

use_cases.title: Set Team Tooling Standards
use_cases.description: Create shared rules for namespacing, schema descriptions, and high-signal responses.

prompt_templates.title: Start a Tool Design
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner planning a first agent-facing tool.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me design an agent-facing tool for [task]. Define the purpose, suggested name, required parameters, and response format.

prompt_templates.title: Review Tool Naming
prompt_templates.scenario: Developer checking a group of related tools.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these tool names for agent clarity and namespacing: [tool list]. Suggest clearer names and explain each change.

prompt_templates.title: Optimize Tool Responses
prompt_templates.scenario: Team reducing token cost and noisy outputs.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this tool response format: [format description]. Recommend pagination, filtering, identifiers, and concise fields for agent workflows.

prompt_templates.title: Audit an MCP Interface
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced review before publishing an MCP server.
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit this MCP tool interface for purpose, schema clarity, output usefulness, token efficiency, and recoverable errors: [tool specification].

output_examples.input: Design a tool for scheduling a meeting.
output_examples.output: A recommended consolidated scheduling tool with availability checks, attendee parameters, clear time constraints, and concise success or conflict responses.
A renamed tool family with service prefixes, consistent action terms, and notes about when each tool should be called.

output_examples.input: Improve a verbose search response for agents.
output_examples.output: A shorter response plan with pagination, filters, human-readable identifiers, and optional detail levels.

best_practices: Design tools around complete agent workflows, not isolated database operations.
Use clear names, parameter descriptions, and valid value constraints.
Return structured, concise results with useful identifiers and recovery guidance.
anti_patterns: Creating many small tools that force agents through repeated calls.
Returning raw identifiers or large data dumps without context.
Writing vague descriptions or errors that do not guide the next action.

faq.question: What does this skill help me build?
faq.answer: It helps you design tools and APIs that AI agents can call reliably and efficiently.

faq.question: Does it generate working MCP server code?
faq.answer: No. It provides design guidance for tool interfaces, schemas, outputs, and validation.

faq.question: Can I use it with Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. It is relevant for Claude, Codex, Claude Code, and other agent tooling workflows.

faq.question: What makes a tool agent-friendly?
faq.answer: Agent-friendly tools have clear names, constrained inputs, useful outputs, and actionable errors.

faq.question: Does it cover security controls?
faq.answer: Only indirectly. You should add separate checks for authentication, authorization, secrets, and abuse prevention.

faq.question: When should I use this skill?
faq.answer: Use it before building a tool, when reviewing an API, or before publishing an MCP interface.
